data.title: Instacart in talks with DoorDash and Uber for sale: report
data.description:
INSTACART is exploring a possible sale and has held preliminary discussions with potential buyers including Uber and DoorDash, The Information reported on Friday (Oct 24), citing people familiar with the matter.

Shares of Instacart closed about 9 per cent higher on Friday. The company had a market value of about US$12 billion as of Thursday’s close.

A potential takeover by Uber or DoorDash could bolster the buyer’s online grocery delivery ambitions by combining Instacart’s established marketplace and retailer ties with its own vast delivery network and customer base.

But either deal could draw antitrust scrutiny, as it would bulk up two of the biggest food-delivery platforms in the US and add to a wave of consolidation. In July, Uber struck a nearly US$15 billion deal to buy Germany’s Delivery Hero.

Shares of Uber closed down around 3 per cent while DoorDash were 4 per cent lower. Instacart declined to comment when contacted by Reuters, while Uber and DoorDash did not immediately respond.

Discussions are ongoing with no guarantee of a deal, the report said, adding that a typical takeover premium of 30 to 40 per cent would value Instacart at roughly US$16 billion to US$17 billion, based on recent public technology deals.

Last year, Instacart lowered its minimum order for free delivery for Instacart+ members to US$10, as rivals DoorDash and Uber Eats expand grocery and convenience delivery. Amazon is also expanding its quick delivery service, Amazon Now, which delivers groceries and essentials in 30 minutes or less.

“Instacart risks getting squeezed between retailers building their own digital channels and larger platforms that can bundle grocery with other services, giving consumers more reasons to keep coming back,” Emarketer analyst Zak Stambor said.

“For Instacart, a deal could provide the resources and reach to compete more effectively than it could on its own,” he said.

In 2021, DoorDash had held talks to acquire Instacart, legally known as Maplebear, in a potential deal that would have valued it between US$40 billion and US$50 billion, The Information had reported. The concerns about Biden administration’s antitrust approval derailed the talks.

Stambor said the latest deal is plausible as the Trump administration has shown “greater willingness” to approve deals even as “it could come at the cost of selling off parts of the business.” REUTERS

data.title: Bringing independent directors into the family boardroom without losing trust
data.description:
FOR many closely held enterprises across Singapore and South-east Asia, inviting non-family directors into the boardroom can feel like sharing the family keys.

It is not that the value of independent perspectives is not recognised. The real challenge is introducing new capabilities without undermining the trusted advisers, family friends and confidants who may have helped build the business.

This concern is a deeply understandable sentiment, and one rooted in genuine pride of ownership.

Yet today, that traditional approach faces an unprecedented inflection point. Across South-east Asia, a vast cohort of family enterprises is preparing for handovers in both ownership and leadership.

Data from HSBC’s global private banking unit indicates that roughly 85 per cent of Asian family owned enterprises will execute a wealth and leadership transfer within the next decade.

At the same time, even as public regulators such as the Singapore Exchange Regulation have progressively raised board-independence standards for listed companies, many middle-market private family firms continue to operate without independent board representation.

As these businesses actively pursue regional expansion, strategic diversification and international capital, not all have established formal non-family oversight equipped to support that cross-border complexity.

The agile, relationship-driven approach of the founding generation worked brilliantly to build these businesses.

However, as ownership becomes increasingly dispersed across generations, operations span multiple jurisdictions, and external capital partners seek greater transparency, informal governance structures are tested in entirely new ways.

Tipping points driving governance reform

In our advisory work with multigenerational family enterprises across the region, we consistently observe four operational crossroads where traditional governance structures reach their limit.

The first involves navigating strategic blind spots. Relying exclusively on internal perspectives over long horizons can naturally narrow a firm’s strategic lens.

For example, as Singapore-based property titans expand internationally, integrating seasoned independent directors with cross-border experience provides essential objectivity when evaluating complex overseas assets.

The second crossroads is the emotional and relational weight of leadership succession. Handovers test family alignment like few other events.

High-profile succession challenges across the region offer a quiet reminder of what can happen when a business lacks neutral arbiters: sensitive family discussions can quickly blur into commercial friction, threatening both value and enterprise reputation.

Independent directors serve as essential shock absorbers, helping depersonalise difficult choices and establishing clear, objective rules of engagement.

Third is the sheer arithmetic of a growing family tree. By the third or fourth generation, balancing diverse family expectations with commercial realities becomes a delicate exercise.

Transitioning to a structured board creates a clear operational boundary, allowing the enterprise to run as a disciplined commercial entity while giving family diplomacy its own dedicated space.

Finally, there is the rising expectation from external capital. Lenders, institutional co-investors, and credit-rating agencies increasingly look for structured oversight.

Singapore’s listed-company governance framework has raised expectations for board independence, creating a benchmark that private firms may increasingly need to consider when seeking sophisticated global growth capital.

Evolving the board while building trust

Welcoming non-family directors does not mean surrendering family control or compromising core values. Instead, it requires a clear playbook built on shared intention rather than rigid corporate formulas.

To start, families should design a board tailored strictly to their strategic priorities, rather than adopting a generic template.

If the next five years are focused on professionalising operations or executing cross-border acquisitions, the board should recruit directors who bring direct, hands-on experience in those exact domains.

Crucially, this evolution does not need to happen overnight; governance is a gradual process of building trust. Board evolution in a family enterprise is rarely a clean-sheet exercise and, often, the most practical route to a stronger board is to add before you subtract.

Consider the example of a second-generation CEO who inherited a board comprising longstanding family friends. While their decades of loyalty carried immense emotional weight, the business had grown significantly more complex.

Simply asking these directors to step down was culturally non-viable and would have felt like a rejection of the relationships that built the firm. Instead, the CEO expanded the board to introduce independent directors with contemporary capabilities, thoughtfully shifting the boardroom dynamic over time without dishonouring historical contributions.

Furthermore, introducing independent perspectives is not about replacing family judgment, but ensuring family judgment is fully informed.

In another family enterprise we worked with, family members occupied several board seats and possessed an intimate understanding of the business. However, some had grown far removed from shifting competitive dynamics, technology shifts and market trends. Board discussions increasingly leaned on historical precedent rather than current data.

By introducing independent directors, the firm brought fresh discipline to the conversation. Assumptions were constructively tested, external benchmarks were introduced, and strategic proposals were backed by market evidence.

Far from diminishing the family’s role, the move allowed family directors to focus on what they do best – stewarding the company’s heritage, values and long-term vision – while grounding every strategic decision in contemporary market reality.

Cultural alignment and emotional intelligence (EI) are non-negotiable qualities that independent directors must have. Technical capability is merely the baseline. They must possess genuine empathy and a deep respect for the family’s legacy, culture and risk tolerance. An adviser lacking high EI may misread subtle family dynamics and fracture trust when sensitive topics arise.

Finally, successful leaders establish clear boundaries between enterprise governance and family governance. Fiduciary boards function best when kept clear of domestic disagreements.

Establishing parallel structures, such as family councils or assemblies, to oversee dividend policies, family charters and next-generation development allows boardroom discussions to remain focused squarely on business strategy and performance.

Preserving legacy through rigour

Inviting independent directors into the inner circle is not a retreat from family stewardship; done thoughtfully, it is one of its highest expressions.

Objective board members bring the candour, market insight and constructive challenge required to navigate an unpredictable global environment, fostering greater resilience.

For family business leaders across South-east Asia, the key question to confront now is whether informal governance has the structural strength and adaptability to support where the family wants to go next.

The writer is Singapore country manager at Russell Reynolds Associates

data.title: Thailand welcomes US-Myanmar engagement, expects Asean talks on countryâs future
data.description:
[LISBON] Thailand welcomes US engagement with Myanmar and expects discussions at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ November summit in Manila on how to proceed with the member barred since the 2021 coup, Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told Reuters on Friday (Oct 24).

The United States and Myanmar’s military-backed government held talks in Tokyo two weeks ago, their second meeting in a month as Washington steps up re-engagement with the generals it shunned after the coup.

“We don’t want to see Myanmar isolated, we don’t want Myanmar to be an arena for geopolitical rivalry ... so the US engagement is something that we welcome,” he said.

Engagement “does not mean legitimising the regime,” but aims to encourage peaceful conflict resolution and reconciliation with the opposition, Phuangketkeow, who is also deputy prime minister, added.

He said there was “some shift in Asean’s position,” citing Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing’s recent visits to Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand and Malaysia, but said it was unclear whether the Manila summit would address restoring Myanmar’s full representation.

“It’s good that we’re going to have a very substantive, very extensive, and very in-depth discussion on how to proceed on Myanmar,” he said.

He also said Thailand and Cambodia could resolve their longstanding land and maritime boundary disputes within 12 to 18 months despite limited progress.

“It is possible, everything is possible,” he said, cautioning that confidence-building and addressing security concerns along the land border, where clashes have occurred, must come first.

Cambodia launched a conciliation process under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea in June to resolve the maritime boundary dispute, after Thailand terminated a 2001 joint development framework in May following deadly border clashes. The first meeting was held about a month ago.

“Right now, we haven’t achieved, to be very frank, much progress,” he said.

The maritime dispute centres on overlapping claims to about 26,000 sq km in the Gulf of Thailand, believed to hold oil and gas reserves worth around US$300 billion. Thailand wants the boundary defined before discussing resource-sharing, he said.

Thailand-EU free-trade talks are in their final stage and could conclude by year-end if there is mutual political will, he added. REUTERS

data.title: OpenAI resumes frontier AI training after security overhaul, discloses flaw in widely used software
data.description:
OPENAI said on Friday (Oct 23) it had resumed training of its most advanced AI models after tightening security and barring internet access, and disclosed a flaw in a widely used software that it found while testing its defences.

The disclosure comes amid concerns over the ability of increasingly capable AI agents to identify and exploit software flaws, including in the guardrails meant to contain them.

OpenAI had paused training of its most capable models after one of its research models used a configuration error to gain limited internet access in September. The company said it contained the incident and used the pause to strengthen its defences.

To test them, OpenAI had teams of AI agents try to break out of their restricted environments. It said the agents found previously unknown flaws, which it had fixed, and training resumed on Oct 1.

During that exercise, the ChatGPT maker found a flaw in Brotli, a widely used data compression tool.

The company said attackers could exploit the flaw by sending malicious data that lets them run their own code on affected systems, including those using popular web software such as Node.js, Bun and Envoy.

OpenAI said the root cause was fixed in Brotli’s source code in February, before it was known to create a security vulnerability, but no new version was released at the time. Brotli has since released updated versions and published a public record of the flaw after OpenAI disclosed it.

Separately on Thursday, AI safety evaluators METR and Redwood Research said they found several new vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s internal system, including an exploit agents could have used to keep hundreds of their actions from being monitored, in a pilot review earlier this year.

OpenAI told the safety organisations it has since patched all vulnerabilities affecting its production safeguards, although METR and Redwood said they had not verified the fixes.

OpenAI has been conducting a broad review of its AI models’ activity since the Hugging Face incident in July, and has informed more than 100 organisations about incidents of unauthorised activity tied to its AI agents. REUTERS

data.title: Fast-fashion groupÂ SheinÂ agrees to pay US$100 million to settle US FTC probe
data.description:
[LONDON] Chinese fast-fashion giant Shein has agreed to pay US$100 million to settle an investigation by the US Federal Trade Commission over delivery delays and other customer complaints, a source with direct knowledge told Reuters on Friday (Oct 24).

The settlement, equivalent to 44 per cent of Shein‘s second-quarter profit, is the latest to hit the online fast-fashion retailer facing a regulatory and tax crackdown in Europe and the US that has slammed the brakes on its growth.

Shein, founded in China though headquartered in Singapore, said in a statement to Reuters that it had “reached a constructive outcome with the FTC”, and that additional information would be shared soon. An FTC spokesperson declined to comment.

The company had warned in July filings for its Hong Kong IPO that the US probe could lead to significant fines.

Consumers filed more than 12,000 complaints about Shein over more than US$11 million in purchases between January 2020 and June 2026, according to FTC records reviewed by Reuters.

At least some of those relate to shipping, with customers reporting to the FTC and Better Business Bureau that they never received packages that Shein had marked as delivered, and that Shein customer service did not resolve the issue.

Reuters was not able to independently verify the substance of the complaints, or whether they were ultimately resolved.

As well as selling its own-brand clothing, Shein‘s website also operates as a marketplace where third-party sellers offer everything from toys to household appliances and decor.

More pain ahead for Shein with higher EU fees

Shein shares have already dropped 22 per cent from their Sep1 listing price as investors realised the extent to which the European Union’s 3-euro fees on low-value e-commerce packages have bruised its business there.

And there’s further pain ahead for Shein, with the EU imposing an additional 2-euro handling fee from Nov 1, making the total fee 5-euro per separate customs code.

“The way these tariffs are implemented is extra punishing for Shein,” said Mike Ryan, head of e-commerce insights at Smarter Ecommerce, who has tracked how Shein has dialled down its spending on Google Ads visibility in Europe.

Shein was known for selling US$5 dresses and US$10 jeans, but has been forced to raise its prices as the US and then Europe closed customs duty loopholes.

CEO Sky Xu said last month that Shein would develop more higher-priced brands in an attempt to boost profitability.

Shein is also still under investigation by the European Commission over illegal products on its marketplace. It was fined 150 million euros (US$168 million) by France’s data protection authority over the improper use of cookies last year.

It’s not the first time the US FTC has taken action against online retailers over deliveries.

US firm Fashion Nova was fined US$9.3 million in 2020 for failing to meet shipping promises to customers and giving them gift cards instead of refunds.

Crocs Inc-owned Hey Dude was also fined US$1.95 million in 2023 for failing to notify customers of shipping delays and suppressing negative reviews. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Stocks to watch: FCT, Olam, OUE Reit
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Oct 22):

Frasers Centrepoint Trust (FCT): The trust posted a distribution per unit (DPU) of S$0.06214 for the second half ended September, up 2.6 per cent from S$0.06059 in the previous corresponding period. This raised total DPU for FY2026 to S$0.1235 – a new high. Revenue for H2 was up 8.7 per cent at S$223 million, and net property income rose 11.5 per cent to S$160.9 million. The increases were driven by contributions from Northpoint City South Wing, as well as higher passing rents across most malls. Units of FCT ended Wednesday 1 per cent or S$0.02 higher at S$2.06.

Olam Group : The group said on Wednesday that neither it nor Olam Agri owns or operates oil palm plantations or concessions in Indonesia. As a result, neither has direct operational exposure to recent forest and peatland fires. It added that Olam Agri ceased to be its subsidiary in April. The group was responding to queries from Singapore Exchange Regulation and said it was unaware of any formal regulatory inquiries or notices relating to Indonesian forest fires contributing to haze. Shares of Olam rose S$0.01 or 1.1 per cent to S$0.91 before the announcement.

OUE Real Estate Investment Trust (Reit) : It posted a 4.6 per cent year-on-year increase in net property income to S$59.6 million for the third quarter ended Sep 30, as stronger hospitality performance offset weaker contributions from its commercial portfolio. Revenue rose 3.1 per cent to S$72.6 million while financing costs fell 12.4 per cent year on year to S$18.9 million, the Reit manager. Units of OUE Reit shed S$0.01 or 2.9 per cent to S$0.33 on Wednesday.

data.title: Stocks to watch: Seatrium, CapitaLand Investment, Keppel DC Reit, Suntec Reit, CLCT, TSH Resources
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Oct 23):

Seatrium : The offshore and marine group has secured a contract from power generation company Karpowership to convert and integrate five hydrogen-ready Whale Class Powerships, each capable of generating up to 600 megawatts of electricity. The first vessel is expected to arrive at Seatrium’s Tuas Boulevard Yard in December 2027. Shares of Seatrium closed S$0.05 or 2.7 per cent lower at S$1.78 on Thursday.

CapitaLand Investment : The real asset manager has appointed banking veteran Hsieh Fu Hua as its independent chairman and non-executive independent director, with effect from Jan 1, 2027. He will succeed Miguel Ko, 73, who will retire as non-executive chairman and non-independent director upon completing his term on Dec 31, the manager announced on Thursday. The manager is also appointing Png Chin Yee, president of Temasek Singapore, as a non-executive, non-independent director from Jan 1. The counter ended 0.9 per cent or S$0.02 lower at S$2.31 on Thursday.

Keppel DC Reit : The real estate investment trust (Reit) on Friday posted a distribution per unit (DPU) of S$0.08571 for the nine-month period ended Sep 30, 2026, up 11.7 per cent from S$0.0767 in the corresponding year-ago period. Distributable income rose 16.7 per cent year on year to S$228 million, while revenue grew 13.3 per cent to S$365.3 million. Units of Keppel DC Reit closed 0.5 per cent or S$0.01 higher at S$2.05 on Thursday.

Suntec Reit : The Reit’s DPU rose 13.4 per cent year on year to S$0.02017 for its third quarter ended Sep 30, from S$0.01778. Revenue was up 5.2 per cent at S$123.6 million. The Reit manager attributed the rise to stronger operating performance across its Singapore office and retail portfolio. Net property income (NPI) grew 6.2 per cent on the year to S$83.4 million from S$78.5 million. The counter closed flat at S$1.36 on Thursday, before the announcement of the results.

CapitaLand China Trust : The Reit on Friday posted NPI of 259.6 million yuan (US$38.9 million) for its third quarter ended Sep 30, 2026, down 5.1 per cent from 273.5 million yuan in the corresponding year-ago period. Revenue for Q3 fell 4.1 per cent year on year to 399.7 million yuan. For the first nine months of 2026, NPI declined 3.9 per cent to 820.6 million yuan, while revenue dropped 4.8 per cent to 1.22 billion yuan. Units of CLCT closed flat on Thursday at S$0.605.

TSH Resources : The plantation company said that 274 hot spots were detected within its estate boundaries in Indonesia between Jan 1 and Oct 21, but maintained that none of the fires occurred within its planted or operational areas. The Malaysian group, which has a primary listing on Bursa Malaysia and a secondary listing on the Singapore Exchange, said all the hot spots were located in community enclaves outside areas directly managed by the company. Shares of TSH Resources closed flat on Thursday at S$0.365.

data.title: OilÂ prices jump US$3 on Houthi attacks,Â oilÂ spill, highest settlement since April
data.description:
[NEW YORK] Oil prices settled more than US$3 higher on Friday (Oct 24), their highest in nearly six months after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East, where UAE authorities also reported an oil spill.

Brent crude futures settled at US$116.72 a barrel, up US$3.55 or 3.14 per cent, their highest since Apr 29. US West Texas Intermediate crude closed at US$103.27 a barrel, up US$3.80 or 3.8 per cent.

Brent finished the week up 6 per cent and WTI ended 2.3 per cent higher.

“Fears of supply disruptions drove the advance after Iranian-backed Houthi rebels carried out a series of attacks across Saudi Arabia, including on energy infrastructure,” said Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist for LPL Financial.

On Thursday, Saudi Aramco ordered the evacuation of its headquarters in Dhahran on the Gulf near Bahrain, Reuters reported. Fighting intensified between Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest crude exporter and Yemen-based Houthis.

An oil spill from a tanker was detected off the UAE coast of Umm Al Quwain, the United Arab Emirates Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said. It did not say what caused the spill and authorities have not identified the tanker involved.

Attacks on vessels

Shipping sources said on Oct 9 that the Gem No. 2 supertanker was struck by an unidentified projectile 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera in the UAE.

“The market is concerned about these continued Iranian attacks on tankers that we’ve seen increase over the last week,” said Andrew Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates. “While there has been an increase in oil transiting out of the Strait of Hormuz, that could change at any minute.”

Clashes between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government have raged since the Iran-aligned Houthis pushed towards Bab el-Mandeb Strait last month, a shipping ​chokepoint at the mouth of the Red Sea.

October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by a Washington-based think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017.

President Donald Trump said on Friday the US could end the war with Iran quickly, but said perhaps Washington should allow the conflict to gradually wind down.

Strategic reserve releases

The US Department of Energy said it had authorized an emergency exchange of up to 400,000 barrels of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to address a supply disruption affecting Phillips 66’s Lake Charles refinery in Louisiana.

The SPR is already at the lowest level since 1982 after President Donald Trump tapped it as the US war on Iran disrupted supply lines. Trump’s predecessor, President Joe Biden, also tapped the SPR following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Elsewhere, Germany’s national oil stockpiling agency EBV circulated a tender to sell diesel, heating oil and crude oil volumes from strategic reserves.

This marks Germany’s first oil releases from strategic reserves since G7 countries, under pressure from Trump, agreed to do so at the start of October.

On Thursday, the head of Libya’s National Oil Corp told Reuters that an oil pipeline valve from the Hamada and Tahara oilfields to Zawiya port had been shut, leading to a reduction in production at both fields.

Ship tracking data showed the first Russian diesel bound for the US since Moscow and Washington reached an export agreement was aboard a tanker heading for New York.

Trump announced the deal this month as part of efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of US midterm elections on Nov 3.

US energy firms this week kept the total rig count unchanged for a second week in a row, energy services firm Baker Hughes said in its closely followed report on Friday.

The total oil and gas rig count, an early indicator of future output, held steady at 603 during the week ended Oct 23. REUTERS

data.title: EuropeanÂ stocks post weekly loss as France turmoil, oil prices dent earnings optimism
data.description:
EUROPEAN stocks suffered their steepest weekly loss since early September, as tensions in France and higher oil prices dampened the optimism sparked by some strong corporate earnings.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 index fell 0.31 per cent to close at 635.77 points on Friday (Oct 24). For the week, the benchmark is down about 1.4 per cent.

The declines cap a week packed with earnings from heavyweights such as SAP, Barclays and Kering, which offered fresh insights into economic conditions and consumer sentiment.

Overall earnings estimates have improved for European companies, but higher crude prices and the unrest in France have left investors jittery.

“What’s happening in France will at least persist as a market factor through the election cycle. The protests might dissipate, but it doesn’t change the financial reality that France is facing,” said Josh Stevens, chief investment officer at CresAlta Investment Management.

The turmoil has provided an explosive backdrop for the presidential election in the country, scheduled for April next year.

Businesses and museums planned to close during the weekend despite curbs on demonstrations as French President Emmanuel Macron seeks to restore order a week after nationwide protests turned violent.

Investors will scrutinise Moody’s decision on France’s credit rating, due later in the day.

Luxury weakness sours sentiment

On Friday, Kering dropped 16.6 per cent after third-quarter sales at its flagship Gucci brand fell. The stock was the biggest laggard on the Stoxx 600, and the luxury index, the worst-performing European sector so far this year, fell 3.6 per cent.

“The European luxury sector continues to suffer from the Middle East war and China’s weakened appetite,” said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote.

L’Oreal climbed 5.6 per cent after the French cosmetics group beat third-quarter sales forecasts.

Defence stocks dropped 3.8 per cent for their worst day since Jun 1, dragged by a 10 per cent decline in French jet engine maker Safran following its results.

The European Central Bank is scheduled to meet next week, with investors pricing in more than a 91 per cent probability that it holds interest rates steady.

The ECB has hiked interest rates twice this year to arrest price pressures stemming from elevated oil prices.

Among other stocks, Holcim gained 5 per cent after the Swiss cement maker raised its full-year earnings forecast, while French food caterer Sodexo rose over 6 per cent after stronger-than-expected full-year revenue.

Volvo Cars slumped over 24 per cent to a record low after reporting a bigger-than-expected third-quarter operating loss and unveiling plans to cut a further 2,500 jobs.

Results from oil majors BP and Shell are due next week. REUTERS

data.title: USÂ stocks: Wall Street closes lower to end rocky week
data.description:
WALL Street’s main indexes closed lower on Friday (Oct 24) even as technology shares steadied somewhat to end a turbulent week for the market-driving AI trade, and investors looked ahead to a busy slate of corporate earnings and a Federal Reserve interest-rate policy meeting.

The Nasdaq Composite posted a slim loss a day after the tech-heavy index suffered its biggest one-day drop since June, as concerns flared over financing costs to support heavy AI investment spending. The S&P 500 technology sector posted a 0.35 per cent gain on Friday.

Most S&P 500 sectors fell, however, including declines of well over 1% for the consumer staples and consumer discretionary groups as well as the financials sector.

Next week, about one-third of S&P 500 companies report quarterly results, including Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, three AI hyperscalers whose capital spending forecasts will be closely watched on Wall Street.

“There is still fallout from the questioning of the AI trade,” said Kristina Hooper, chief market strategist at Man Group. “There’s certainly the potential that we see less invested in an AI data center build-out next year than has been projected. So I certainly think that’s giving pause.”

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 652.82 points, or 1.23 per cent, to 52,215.16; the S&P 500 lost 39.75 points, or 0.52 per cent, to 7,623.68 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 53.52 points, or 0.21 per cent, to 25,955.34.

For the week, the S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent and the Nasdaq dropped 0.7 per cent. The blue-chip Dow rose 0.4 per cent, its third straight weekly gain.

Telecommunications stocks fell, weighing on the communication services sector, after a report that SpaceX was seeking thousands of cell sites for a fourth wireless carrier.

Shares of AT&T and T-Mobile both sank nearly 8 per cent while Verizon shed 1.2 per cent. SpaceX shares rose 1.9 per cent. US cell tower operators gained, with Crown Castle up 9 per cent and American Tower up 4 per cent.

The energy sector rose 2.5 per cent, hitting a record high. Brent crude hit its highest level since late April, after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concern over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East.

American Express shares fell 3.7 per cent, weighing on the Dow. The company raised its profit forecast as it also announced plans to eliminate 5 per cent of its workforce.

SLB shares rose 7 per cent after the oilfield services provider beat Wall Street estimates for third-quarter profit.

Data from the University of Michigan showed US consumer sentiment edged down near a record low in October, as rising prices because of the Middle East conflict soured households’ views of the economy.

Market focus remains on the earnings season, with robust corporate profit growth underpinning gains for major equity indexes this year. S&P 500 companies are on track to have increased earnings by more than 32 per cent in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES data.

The Fed is expected to keep interest rates steady when it gives its policy statement on Wednesday, but investors will be eager for clues about whether the US central bank will hike rates at its December meeting.

Wall Street is also increasingly focused on the Nov 3 midterm elections, which will decide control of the US Congress.

Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.72-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange. On the Nasdaq, declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.57-to-1 ratio.

The S&P 500 posted 18 new 52-week highs and 8 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 74 new highs and 334 new lows.

Volume on US exchanges was 15.4 billion shares, compared with the 17.2 billion average over the last 20 trading days. REUTERS
